page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: Isochores are the curves obtained when the
pressure of a gas is plotted against its
steps.why: Iso means same and chore comes from the Greek word for space: one curve collects all the P–T states of the gas that share one volume.
common_mistakes: Naming the wrong pair of axes. Isochores are P against T.
steps.memory_tip: The three constants cover the three variables once each: isotherm holds T, isobar holds P, isochore holds V. Whatever is held constant, the other two are plotted.
steps.margin_note: Axes (P against T) plus constant volume make the definition.

steps.label: The constant quantity

lines.text: Isochore: a P–T curve of a gas at constant volume

lines: Along one isochore P ∝ T for an ideal gas,
so the curve is a straight line.
steps.why: At fixed volume the pressure of an ideal gas grows in step with the absolute temperature (P ∝ T), so an ideal-gas isochore is a straight line, exactly as the isobar is on the V–T plot.
common_mistakes: Assigning PV = constant here. That is the isotherm's law, not the isochore's.
steps.memory_tip: Fixed box, rising temperature: the pressure climbs in a straight line.
steps.margin_note: P ∝ T at constant V is sometimes named Amontons' law or Gay-Lussac's pressure law; the relation matters more than the name.

insider_note: Of the three curve definitions, isochore is the one students mix up most — fix it as the LAST pairing left over: V constant, P against T.
